facts.note: The figure of record: the flat's long axis is 80 blocks, from the wake point to the gatehouse's foot.
The cross axis is 40 blocks.
Heights are metres against the standing tide, 0.0, the datum tide.md fixes. Every image and every elevation below is drawn at that level.
Seven stacked ground planes, and they are not one plane. A composition that lays these out at a single level has not built Halgrave.
Massing table: the flat, floor -1.2 -- tidal sand, cairns, iron stakes, the causeway running off south.
Massing table: the ward, -1.5 floor -- the drowned outer ward, a basin below the gate that admits it.
Massing table: the ward, +0.4 causeway top -- the raised spine across the drowned ward, the water on both sides.
Massing table: the gate, floor +2.5 -- the gatehouse passage, in the rock's south foot.
Massing table: the road, floor +4.0 -- the cut ledge on the west cliff, above and outside everything.
Massing table: the cloister, floor +9 -- the chapel ward's paving, on the upper shelf.
Massing table: the hall, floor +12 -- the keep's floor, the one intact roof.
Massing table: the ramp and belfry, +14 / +30 -- the upper ward's cobbles, and the belfry floor above them. This fact takes the first half of that row: the upper ward's cobbles at +14.
Massing table: the ramp and belfry, +14 / +30 -- the upper ward's cobbles, and the belfry floor above them. This fact takes the second half of that row: the belfry floor at +30.
The cistern is under the upper half of all of this, floor at -0.15.
The cistern is under the upper half of all of this, floor at -0.15, its well's silt bed at -2.3.

The ward is a hole, not a floor. Its floor is four metres below the gate sill that opens onto it, which is the whole reason it has been sea for fifty-one years. Drawn level with the gate it is a courtyard and the campaign has no drowned ward.
The cistern is beneath, not beside. Its grille comes out in the ward's rock face 1.3 above the ward floor, at the height the water used to stand.

The tower is a climb, not a room. tide.md puts its approach at +14 and its belfry floor at +30: sixteen metres of tower between a player's feet at the door and the floor they ring from, with a broken first flight in it.
Above it stands the belfry storey, which is a room walked around a bell that is itself a structure -- five metres of bell and frame, two of headroom over the ring, two of cap.
Five metres of bell and frame, two of headroom over the ring, two of cap.
Five metres of bell and frame, two of headroom over the ring, two of cap.
Five metres of bell and frame, two of headroom over the ring, two of cap -- so the crown is at +39.
The tower, standing clear of all of it, twice the height of anything else, plain and square and unbuttressed.
The flat is at -1.2 and a standing player's eye is 1.62 above the ground they stand on, so the eye is at +0.42.
The eye is at +0.42 and the crown stands 38.58 m above it.
A building is read as one whole object, rather than as detail or as landscape, when it subtends about 27 degrees in the vertical.
At 38.58 m of height that is 38.58 / tan 27 deg = 75.7 m.
Checked a second way, by the ratio rule from a different source rather than by the same tangent: the same reading is conventionally written D/H = 2, which gives 2 x 38.58 = 77.2 m.
The two land 1.9% apart, which is what says neither is a units error.
The answer moves 1.96 m per metre of crown height, so a crown three metres out either way still gives 70-82 m; the number is robust at the scale of the decision.
Minecraft's default field of view is 70 deg vertical, so at a level gaze the crown falls outside the frame nearer than 38.58 / tan 35 deg = 55.1 m.
The belfry has to see the flat's far end in one downward look, and a 31.2 m drop at 10 deg of depression reaches 177 m.
The recognition feature -- the square hole of sky with the bell in it -- stays legible on a 1080p screen out to 321 m, so legibility is not the binding constraint at any length the flat could have.
Minecraft's horizontal field of view is 102.5 deg on a 16:9 screen, so from a standpoint 20 blocks back the frame is 20 x tan 51.2 deg = 24.9 blocks to each side.
From a standpoint 20 blocks back the frame is 20 x tan 51.2 deg = 24.9 blocks to each side: a 40-wide stake line fits, and a wider one does not.
Standing on the flat at the causeway head, looking north, the player sees five bands stacked.
The site is a compact stepped mass, not a chain. Z0, Z1, Z2, Z3, Z4, Z5 and the cistern's collapse shaft must all fall inside one downward view from the tower's top.
